title: National screening programmes
blurb: Explain what screening can and cannot do, what a screen-positive result means, and who is offered which NHS programme in England.
question: Mrs Achterberg, 62, lives in England. She feels well, but her friend has just been treated for bowel cancer and she wants to know which NHS screening she should be having, how often, and what a 'positive' result would mean. What should the nurse tell her?

teach.h: What screening is, and what it is not
teach.body: Screening is a way of identifying apparently healthy people who may have an increased risk of a particular condition, so that early treatment or information can be offered. It is not a diagnosis. A screen-positive (higher-risk) result means the person may have the condition and is offered diagnostic tests to confirm it. A screen-negative result means low risk now, not that the condition can never develop.

teach.caption: An independent expert group, the UK National Screening Committee, advises the NHS in all four UK countries which programmes to offer, and recommends screening only when benefits outweigh harms.

head: Programme
Who
How often / test
rows: Women and people with a cervix 25–64
Men in the year they turn 65
Lung health check, then CT if higher risk
teach.caption: Over the age range: bowel 75+ can ask for a kit every 2 years; breast 71+ can self-refer every 3 years; men over 65 can self-refer for AAA.
Some deaths from AAA, bowel, breast and cervical cancer can be prevented. Screening tests are not 100% accurate.

teach.body: A screen-negative result does not protect against developing the condition later, and screening can miss a problem. A person with symptoms, such as rectal bleeding or a breast lump, should see their GP whatever their last screening result and whenever their next invitation is due. False reassurance from a recent normal result is a recognised risk of false negatives.

items.label: AAA scan for men; cervical ends

items: Bowel: FIT checks a poo sample for blood; the first kit arrives at 50, 52 or 54 depending on when the person turned 50.
Breast: first invitation between 50 and 53; people taking feminising hormones for over 2 years can have screening.
Cervical: changed from 3-yearly to 5-yearly; people may be recalled sooner if HPV is found.
AAA: result given at the end of the scan; no aneurysm means no further scans; small ones are rescanned yearly and medium ones every 3 months.
Diabetic eye: every year, or every 2 years if the last 2 tests showed no changes; gestational diabetes is not invited.

teach.h: Scenario: Mrs Achterberg at the practice
teach.body: Practice nurse Joy explains that at 62 Mrs Achterberg is offered bowel screening with a FIT home kit every 2 years, breast screening every 3 years and cervical screening every 5 years until 64. A screen-positive result is not a diagnosis; it means she will be offered tests, such as a colonoscopy, to find out. Joy adds that if she ever notices symptoms, such as bleeding or a change in bowel habit, she should see the GP straight away rather than wait for her next kit.

teach.text: Don't confuse the intervals: bowel every 2 years, breast every 3 years, cervical every 5 years. And don't treat a screen-positive result as a diagnosis, or a screen-negative result as a guarantee.

items: Screening identifies increased risk in apparently healthy people; it is a choice, not a diagnosis.
Screen positive → diagnostic tests; screen negative → low risk now.
Bowel 50–74 FIT every 2 years; breast 50 to 71st birthday every 3 years; cervical 25–64 every 5 years.
AAA: men in the year they turn 65; lung: 55–74 who have ever smoked; diabetic eye from 12.
UK NSC advises all four UK nations; benefits must outweigh harms.
Symptoms need a GP review regardless of a recent normal screen.

summary: You can now explain the purpose, benefits and limits of screening and what screen-positive and screen-negative results mean. You can also state who is offered each adult NHS screening programme in England and how often.

A.q: In England, how often is a person aged 50–74 sent a bowel cancer screening FIT kit?
A.why: NHS: people aged 50 to 74 registered with a GP are sent a FIT kit every 2 years.

whyNot.0: Annual recall applies to some diabetic eye screening, not bowel screening.
whyNot.2: Every 3 years is the breast screening interval.
whyNot.3: Every 5 years is the cervical screening interval.

A.q: Who is invited for abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) screening in England?
options: Men in the year they turn 65
A.why: NHS: all men living in England are invited for AAA screening in the year they turn 65; men over 65 can self-refer.

whyNot.0: Women are not routinely invited, and the age is 65.
whyNot.1: Smoking history determines lung screening eligibility, not AAA invitation.
whyNot.2: AAA invitation is by sex and age, not by hypertension; people at higher risk can discuss a scan with their GP.

A.q: Grace, 34, has a screen-positive result from cervical screening. What does this mean?
options: She has cervical cancer and needs treatment
The test was faulty and must be repeated
She may have it and will be offered further tests
She is at no further risk until her next invitation
A.why: A screen-positive (higher-risk) result means the person may have the condition; diagnostic tests are offered to confirm it (NHS screening).

whyNot.0: Screening is not diagnostic; further tests are needed.
whyNot.1: A positive result is a finding, not a fault.
whyNot.3: This describes a reassuring result, not a positive one.

B.q: Mr Kowal, 57, returned a FIT kit four months ago and the result was normal. He now mentions a change in bowel habit for five weeks and some weight loss he cannot explain. What should the nurse advise?
options: See his GP promptly about these symptoms
Wait for his next FIT kit, as his last result was normal
Request an extra FIT kit from the screening helpline
Increase his fibre intake and review in three months
B.why: Screening can miss a problem and a normal result does not mean the condition cannot develop. New symptoms need prompt GP assessment regardless of screening (NHS screening).

whyNot.1: Waiting for screening ignores symptoms that need assessment now.
whyNot.2: Screening is for people without symptoms; symptomatic people need clinical assessment.
whyNot.3: Delaying review of red flag symptoms is unsafe.

B.q: Dorothy, 72, attended every breast screening appointment she was sent. She tells the nurse that the letters seem to have stopped and asks whether she is still entitled to mammograms. What is accurate?
options: Screening stops completely after the age of 70
She will be invited yearly from now on
She needs a GP referral for each mammogram
B.why: NHS: automatic invitations stop at the 71st birthday, but women 71 and over can still have screening every 3 years by contacting their local breast screening service.

whyNot.1: There is no annual invitation; the interval stays 3 years.
whyNot.2: She contacts the breast screening service directly; a GP referral is not needed.

B.q: Which person meets the age and smoking criteria for NHS lung cancer screening in England?
options: A 78-year-old who has smoked for 50 years
A 65-year-old non-smoker with a family history
A 60-year-old who stopped smoking 15 years ago
B.why: NHS: people aged 55 to 74 who have ever smoked may be invited for a lung health check, with CT if at higher risk.

whyNot.0: At 52 he is below the 55 starting age.
whyNot.1: At 78 she is above the upper age of 74.
whyNot.2: The programme is for people who have ever smoked.

C.q: Mo, 14, has type 1 diabetes. His last two diabetic eye screening tests showed no changes. How often will he now be invited?
C.why: NHS: people with diabetes aged 12 or over are invited every year, or every 2 years if their last 2 tests found no changes.

whyNot.0: Six-monthly is not a routine screening interval.
whyNot.1: Yearly applies until two consecutive tests show no changes.
whyNot.3: Five years is the cervical screening interval.

C.q: Mr Lindqvist, 48, has seen an advert for a private 'total body MRI health check' and asks the nurse whether it would be better than waiting for NHS screening. Which response is most accurate?
options: Private tests are generally more accurate than NHS screening
Private scans replace the need for NHS screening
Some private tests lack evidence that benefits outweigh harms
The UK NSC recommends whole-body scans for adults after 50
C.why: NHS: private companies offer tests, some not recommended by the UK NSC because it is not clear that benefits outweigh harms such as false positives and unnecessary tests.

whyNot.0: Accuracy is not guaranteed and false positives can lead to unnecessary tests.
whyNot.1: Private tests do not replace NHS programmes.
whyNot.3: The UK NSC does not recommend whole-body screening scans.

C.q: Ahmed, 66, had AAA screening last year and no aneurysm was found. He asks when his next scan will be. What is accurate?
C.why: NHS: if no aneurysm is found, the person does not need any more scans.

whyNot.1: Yearly scans are for small aneurysms.
whyNot.2: Three-monthly scans are for medium aneurysms.
whyNot.3: There is no routine 5-year rescan after a normal result.

reteach.question: How can you remember the three cancer screening intervals?

blocks.body: Bowel (low in the body): every 2 years, ages 50–74, home FIT kit. Breast (higher): every 3 years, 50 to the 71st birthday. Cervix: every 5 years, 25–64. Then one-off and special programmes: AAA scan for men in the year they turn 65; lung checks for people 55–74 who have ever smoked; diabetic eye screening every 1–2 years from 12.

blocks.text: A screen-positive result means 'more tests', not 'you have it'.

explain.body: Screening finds increased risk in apparently healthy people. Positive: offered diagnostic tests. Negative: low risk now. It is always a choice, supported by an information leaflet.

test.q: Who advises the NHS in all four UK countries on which screening programmes to offer?
options: The Chief Medical Officer for England
test.why: NHS: the UK National Screening Committee, an independent expert group, advises the NHS in all 4 UK countries.

whyNot.1: NICE produces clinical guidance but does not decide national screening programmes.
whyNot.3: The CMO advises government broadly; screening recommendations come from the UK NSC.

explain.body: Bowel: everyone 50–74, FIT every 2 years (75+ on request). Breast: women 50 to 71st birthday, every 3 years (71+ self-refer). Cervical: 25–64, every 5 years.

test.q: What is the age range and interval for routine cervical screening in England?
test.why: NHS: women and people with a cervix aged 25 to 64 are invited every 5 years.

whyNot.0: This describes the previous 3-yearly interval for younger people, which has changed to 5 years.

explain.body: AAA: men in the year they turn 65, one ultrasound; over 65 self-refer. Lung: 55–74 who have ever smoked: lung health check, CT if higher risk.

test.q: What test is used for NHS AAA screening?
test.why: NHS AAA screening is a quick ultrasound scan of the abdomen.

whyNot.0: CT is used in lung screening, not AAA screening.
whyNot.1: An X-ray is not the screening test and does not reliably measure the aorta.
whyNot.2: No blood test is used to screen for AAA.

explain.body: Everyone with diabetes aged 12 or over: photographs of the back of the eye every year, or every 2 years after two normal tests. Gestational diabetes is not invited.

test.q: From what age are people with diabetes offered diabetic eye screening in England?
test.why: NHS: from the age of 12, all people with diabetes are offered diabetic eye screening.

whyNot.0: Young children are not screened by this programme.
whyNot.3: Waiting to 40 would miss years of possible retinopathy.
